absent: Full layouts of migration groups, per CPU migration state and migration events.
Construction of hierarchy levels, parent links and cross node grouping.
Behavior of upward walk driver and remote expiry handler invoked during remote handling.
Timer wheel mechanics including base forwarding, insertion, detachment and expiry computation.
Meanings and values of wheel sizing and base mask constants beyond those shown.
Posix CPU timer work setup and timer soft interrupt handler internals.
Hrtimer, clock base, tick device and scheduler structure definitions and valid state values.
Availability mask management and hierarchy mutex critical sections.
Trace event definitions and payloads for migration activity.
Proc sequence file error handling and concurrency guarantees.

findings.text: Remote handling for migrated timers is offered as a per CPU operation that refreshes the local wakeup estimate from the group hierarchy, while a header definition provides the same named operation as having no effect.
Per CPU timer wheel lifecycle provides preparation that initializes clocks and expiry state for a given CPU and a dead CPU handover that relocates all queued timers to the surviving CPU.
Boot initialization establishes per CPU timer bases for every possible CPU and completes setup of related work plus registration of the timer soft interrupt handler.
Group event maintenance for the migration hierarchy is exposed for upward propagation of expiry changes, with the new timer path sharing the same propagation behavior.
Timer diagnostics are available through a readable status listing and through a synchronous console dump that reports per CPU clocks and tick devices.
Status listing uses sequence iteration with start next stop and show operations that first enumerate online CPUs and then tick devices when that support is present.
Listing iterator state consists of a CPU identifier where a negative value denotes header position plus a flag selecting the second enumeration pass and a captured timestamp taken at iteration start.
Hierarchy walk context carries requested and discovered expiry values plus an event reference, a child selection mask, remote and check indicators, and base time values for the walk.

Migration hierarchy configuration comprises level counts, per CPU state instances, an availability mask with associated mutex, a global management mutex and a static key controlling isolated CPU treatment.
A child may act as migrator only when the recorded migrator equals its own mask or when no migrator is recorded.

Remote handling publishes the discovered earliest expiry as the CPU wakeup value only at the end under lock and tolerates a stale value in between because callers run in interrupt context with deferred tick evaluation.
Remote handling returns promptly without hierarchy traversal when the local CPU is not the migrator and no wakeup is pending.
Newly prepared timer bases start from current tick time with a far future next expiry and with pending, recalculation and idle indicators cleared.
Timers relocated to another CPU have their base association rewritten to the destination CPU before reinsertion.
Isolation treatment is disabled unless a dedicated static key is enabled, after which membership depends on housekeeping domain and kernel noise attributes.
Each group caches the expiry of its earliest non ignorable event, resetting to the maximum value when no such event exists and lazily discarding ignorable entries while the cache is refreshed.
Activation marks the child bit active, claims migratorship when vacant, advances a sequence count and retires the local group event from parent consideration.
When the top group has no parent and no migrator, an update computes the earliest group expiry for global handling unless the update occurs as part of remote handling.
Diagnostic printing directs output to the sequence file when available and to the kernel log otherwise.
Per clock active timer reporting adjusts the captured time by the clock offset before computing remaining time.

Tick device diagnostics distinguish broadcast from per CPU devices and report clock event parameters including limits, scaling, state, pending event, callbacks and retry counts plus wakeup device when broadcast is available.
Per CPU diagnostics enumerate all clock bases with address, index, resolution and offset where applicable before reporting high resolution and tick scheduler state and global tick time.
Compilation unit defines a tracepoint creation marker.
Remote wakeup publication holds the per CPU migration lock in interrupt disabled form only for the final store.
Dead CPU timer handover acquires the destination base lock with interrupts disabled and then the source base lock in nested form, relying on global serialization of the caller to avoid deadlock.
Group event lookup requires the group lock to be held by the caller.
Hierarchy event updates lock child then parent in nested order when a child is present and only the group otherwise, releasing in reverse order.
Active timer diagnostics lock the clock base with interrupts saved for each single entry copy and release before formatting output, repeating from the head to the next index.
Migration management provides a global mutex and a separate availability mutex alongside an availability mask.
Group migratorship moves between vacant and owned by a child mask, with activation claiming vacancy and later updates preserving ownership according to activity.

Group events cycle between queued with a concrete expiry, ignored when the subtree is empty or active, and removed upon expiry or replacement, with upward propagation required after remote handling even when ignorable.
Status listing iteration progresses from header to each online CPU in identifier order, then when enabled switches to a second pass for broadcast header and per CPU tick devices before terminating.
Clearing a dead CPU running timer pointer after emitting a one time warning signals unexpected handler state during teardown.
Lockless retirement of group events on activation may cause a parent migrator to perform a redundant remote expiry if it observes the change late, which is tolerated as harmless.
Concurrent activation may race event updates and cause a useless remote expiry to be scheduled, which the design accepts.
Diagnostic enumeration of active timers revisits the queue from the start for each entry, giving quadratic cost on long queues in exchange for not holding the base lock during output.
Live CPU and tick scheduler counters in diagnostics are read without full synchronization and may be stale or inconsistent.
No migrator marker has value 255 and child mask width is 8.
Status listing is registered under name timer_list with numeric mode 0400 and its header reports version v0.11 plus the count of clock bases.
